hld-video-uber:0.prompt: A creator uploads a 3 GB video from a phone on a flaky mobile network. Why should the upload API accept the file as resumable chunks instead of one HTTP request?
options: Chunks let the CDN start caching the video before upload finishes
A dropped connection only loses the in-flight chunk, so the client resumes from the last acknowledged one
Object storage cannot store any single object larger than 1 GB
Chunking compresses the video so less data crosses the network
hld-video-uber:0.explanation: Resumable chunked uploads (e.g. S3 multipart, tus) track which parts arrived, so a network drop costs one chunk rather than restarting 3 GB. Object stores do support multi-GB objects, and chunking itself does no compression.

hld-video-uber:0.prompt: Why do upload services typically hand the client a pre-signed object-storage URL rather than streaming the video bytes through the API servers?
options: Pre-signed URLs make the uploaded file publicly readable by default
It is the only way to attach metadata such as the title to a video
It keeps gigabytes of traffic off the stateless API tier while still authorizing the upload
API servers cannot terminate TLS for large request bodies
hld-video-uber:0.explanation: The API authenticates the user and signs a short-lived URL scoped to one key; the bytes then go straight to object storage, so API servers aren't tied up proxying huge bodies. Pre-signed upload URLs don't make objects public, and metadata goes through the normal API.

hld-video-uber:0.prompt: In HLS or MPEG-DASH adaptive bitrate streaming, which component decides which bitrate rendition to fetch next?
options: The origin server, based on its current CPU load
The CDN edge, based on the cache hit ratio
The transcoder, which embeds one fixed choice in the manifest
The client player, based on measured throughput and buffer level
hld-video-uber:0.explanation: ABR is client-driven: the manifest lists all renditions and the player picks the next segment's rendition from its own throughput estimate and buffer state. Servers and CDNs just serve plain HTTP GETs for whatever segment is requested.

hld-video-uber:0.prompt: A 2-hour movie takes 4 hours to transcode on one machine. What is the standard way to cut this to minutes?
options: Split the source into short segments, transcode them in parallel on many workers, then stitch the outputs
Transcode only the 1080p rendition and let clients downscale it themselves
Use a faster disk so the encoder reads the source file more quickly
Delay transcoding until the first viewer presses play, then encode on demand
hld-video-uber:0.explanation: Transcoding is CPU-bound and parallelizes well when the source is split at keyframe boundaries into independent chunks fed to a worker pool (a DAG of split, encode, merge). Disk speed isn't the bottleneck, and encoding on first play would make the first viewer wait.

hld-video-uber:0.prompt: Transcoding workers pull jobs from a queue and sometimes crash mid-job. What makes the pipeline reliable without producing corrupt or duplicate output?
options: Delete each job from the queue as soon as a worker receives it
Use at-least-once delivery (visibility timeout) with idempotent outputs keyed by video, rendition and segment
Run every job on two workers simultaneously and keep whichever finishes first
Have a single coordinator machine run all jobs serially so crashes are rare
hld-video-uber:0.explanation: If the worker dies, the message becomes visible again and another worker retries it; writing output to a deterministic key means a retry overwrites rather than duplicates. Deleting on receipt loses jobs on crash, and running every job twice doubles cost without fixing partial writes.

hld-video-uber:0.prompt: Why must keyframes (IDR frames) be aligned at the same timestamps across all renditions of a video in an ABR ladder?
options: Aligned keyframes are required for the CDN to compute cache keys
Without alignment the audio track would drift out of sync
So each segment starts with a keyframe at the same time in every rendition, letting the player switch at segment boundaries
Aligned keyframes reduce the file size of the highest-bitrate rendition
hld-video-uber:0.explanation: A segment can only be decoded independently if it begins with a keyframe. When segment N starts at the same instant in every rendition, the player can switch from 720p segment N-1 to 1080p segment N seamlessly. Audio sync and cache keys don't depend on this.

hld-video-uber:0.prompt: A team proposes cutting HLS segment duration from 6 s to 1 s. What is the main trade-off?
options: Faster startup and bitrate adaptation, but more HTTP requests, manifest churn and slightly worse compression
Better compression efficiency, but the player can no longer switch bitrates mid-stream
Lower CDN request rate, but much higher latency for live streams
No real trade-off: shorter segments are strictly better
hld-video-uber:0.explanation: Short segments let the player react sooner and reduce live latency, but each segment needs its own request and starts with a keyframe, which costs bits. 6x more requests also raises per-request overhead at the CDN. Request rate goes up, not down.

hld-video-uber:0.prompt: Which of these are typical outputs of a VOD transcoding pipeline? Select all that apply.
options: Several renditions at different resolutions and bitrates
A manifest or playlist (e.g. .m3u8 or .mpd) listing the renditions and segments
Thumbnail or preview images
Each viewer's bandwidth estimate for future playback
One single high-bitrate MP4 served identically to every device
hld-video-uber:0.explanation: The pipeline produces a bitrate ladder, manifests that describe it, and artwork such as thumbnails. Bandwidth estimates are measured live by each player, and serving one file to everyone is exactly what ABR exists to avoid.

hld-video-uber:0.prompt: Which signals do client-side ABR algorithms commonly use to choose the next segment's bitrate? Select all that apply.
options: Throughput measured while downloading recent segments
How many seconds of video are currently buffered
The size of the original file the creator uploaded
How many other people are watching the same video
hld-video-uber:0.explanation: Throughput-based and buffer-based algorithms (and hybrids) use exactly these two signals. The original upload's size and global viewer counts tell the player nothing about its own network conditions.

hld-video-uber:0.prompt: In HLS, the server pushes each next segment to the player at the bitrate it has chosen for that viewer.
options: True
False
hld-video-uber:0.explanation: False. HLS is pull-based: the player downloads the playlist and issues plain HTTP GETs for segments it picks. That is why HLS works through ordinary CDNs and caches without server-side session state.

hld-video-uber:0.prompt: For a very popular video, spending much more CPU on a slower, higher-compression encode can pay off, because encoding is paid once while bandwidth savings repeat on every view.
options: True
False
hld-video-uber:0.explanation: True. Encode cost is fixed per video, while egress cost scales with views. That's why large platforms use per-title encoding or newer codecs (VP9, AV1) for popular content, and cheaper encodes for the long tail that few people watch.

hld-video-uber:1.prompt: Video segments are immutable once transcoded. What caching policy fits them best at the CDN?
options: Short TTL (a few seconds) so edits propagate quickly
No caching, so view counts stay accurate
Cache only at the origin, never at the edge
Long TTL with versioned or content-addressed URLs, since a segment's bytes never change
hld-video-uber:1.explanation: Immutable content can be cached for a very long time (e.g. Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable). If content does change, it gets a new URL. Short TTLs just cause needless revalidation, and view counts shouldn't rely on CDN misses.

hld-video-uber:1.prompt: A platform has a few thousand hugely popular videos and millions of rarely watched ones. Which CDN strategy is most cost-effective?
options: Push every video to every edge location at upload time
Pre-position popular content at edges and let long-tail videos be fetched from regional caches or origin on demand
Serve everything from origin and use the CDN only for thumbnails
Pick a random subset of videos to cache at each edge
hld-video-uber:1.explanation: Popularity follows a power law. Edge storage is limited, so you proactively place the head of the distribution near users and pull tail content on demand through a cache hierarchy. Pushing everything everywhere wastes storage on videos nobody watches.

hld-video-uber:1.prompt: Each view runs `UPDATE videos SET views = views + 1 WHERE id = ?`. A viral video gets 50k views/s and the database falls over. What is the standard fix?
options: Put a unique index on the views column
Switch the column type to BIGINT
Emit view events to a stream, aggregate counts in short windows, and write batched increments
Run the UPDATE inside SERIALIZABLE transactions
hld-video-uber:1.explanation: A single hot row turns into a lock-contention bottleneck. Buffering events and flushing periodic aggregates (e.g. +48,213 every few seconds) cuts writes by orders of magnitude. SERIALIZABLE would make contention worse, and the column type isn't the issue.

hld-video-uber:1.prompt: Product wants an approximate count of unique viewers per video per day using little memory. Which structure fits?
options: HyperLogLog
Bloom filter
Count-min sketch
A sorted set of viewer IDs
hld-video-uber:1.explanation: HyperLogLog estimates cardinality (distinct count) in a few KB with ~1% error. Redis has it built in as PFADD/PFCOUNT. A Bloom filter answers membership rather than counts, count-min estimates per-item frequency, and a set of IDs uses memory that grows with viewers.

hld-video-uber:1.prompt: A highly anticipated video goes live and thousands of edge servers miss on the same segments at the same moment, flooding the origin. Which mitigation targets this directly?
options: Lower the segment TTL so edges refresh more often
Add more replicas of the metadata database
Disable HTTP/2 between edges and origin
Use an origin-shield tier and request coalescing so one miss per segment reaches the origin
hld-video-uber:1.explanation: Request collapsing makes concurrent misses for the same object wait on a single upstream fetch, and an origin shield funnels all edges through one mid-tier cache. A lower TTL would cause more misses, and the metadata DB isn't on the segment path.

hld-video-uber:1.prompt: Why do large video platforms often show a view count that lags behind or freezes for a while on new videos?
options: The CDN hides view requests from the application servers
Counting happens in an asynchronous pipeline that also filters bots and invalid views before publishing totals
SQL databases can't store numbers above a few million
Counts are only recomputed when the creator logs in
hld-video-uber:1.explanation: Views pass through an async pipeline (stream, dedup and fraud checks, then aggregation) so that only valid views count. The displayed number is eventually consistent. Freshness is traded for accuracy and lower write load. It has nothing to do with database limits.

hld-video-uber:1.prompt: Paid videos must not be playable by anyone who copies a segment URL. What is the usual CDN-friendly approach?
options: Have the CDN call the auth service on every segment request
Serve paid content from origin only, bypassing the CDN
Issue short-lived signed URLs or signed cookies that the edge can verify without contacting origin
Rename segment files every hour
hld-video-uber:1.explanation: The edge checks an HMAC or signature and an expiry locally, so access control scales with the CDN. Calling auth on every segment adds latency and load, and bypassing the CDN gives up its whole benefit.

hld-video-uber:1.prompt: Which changes improve the CDN cache hit ratio for video segments? Select all that apply.
options: Normalizing the cache key to ignore irrelevant query parameters
Adding an origin-shield tier between edges and origin
Embedding a per-user session ID in every segment URL
Sending Cache-Control: no-store on segments
Using long TTLs for immutable segments
hld-video-uber:1.explanation: Fewer distinct keys, a shared mid-tier, and long lifetimes all raise hits. A per-user token inside the cache key makes every user's segment a different object (use signed cookies or ignore the token in the key instead), and no-store disables caching entirely.

hld-video-uber:1.prompt: View events go through a Kafka-style partitioned log before aggregation. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: The log can be replayed to recompute counts after a bug in the aggregator
Partitioning by videoId lets one consumer own each video's running count
The log alone guarantees exactly-once increments in the database, with no idempotence needed
Ingestion and aggregation are decoupled, so a slow aggregator doesn't drop events
hld-video-uber:1.explanation: A durable log gives you replay, key-based ownership and backpressure isolation. End-to-end exactly-once still needs idempotent or transactional sinks (e.g. storing consumer offsets with the counts). The log by itself only provides at-least-once delivery to the DB.

hld-video-uber:1.prompt: Partitioning view events by videoId avoids cross-partition coordination for a video's count, but a viral video can turn its partition into a hotspot.
options: True
False
hld-video-uber:1.explanation: True. Key-based partitioning sends all of one key's events to one partition. For extreme keys you can salt the key (videoId#0..N), pre-aggregate on producers, and then merge the sub-counts.

hld-video-uber:1.prompt: In a YouTube-style design, exact real-time view counts are a hard requirement, so eventual consistency for the counter is unacceptable.
options: True
False
hld-video-uber:1.explanation: False. View counts are the classic example of data that can be approximate and lag by seconds or minutes. Accepting eventual consistency is what allows batching, fraud filtering and cheap writes.

hld-video-uber:2.prompt: A rider sits near the edge of a geohash cell. Why does a 'find nearby drivers' query look at the rider's cell plus its 8 neighbors?
options: Geohash cells overlap, so drivers are stored in several cells
Neighbor lookups are needed to decode the geohash back into latitude/longitude
Points that are physically close can fall in adjacent cells with different prefixes
Redis requires at least nine keys per geospatial query
hld-video-uber:2.explanation: A shared prefix implies proximity, but the reverse isn't true: two points a few meters apart across a cell boundary can have very different geohashes. Querying the 3x3 block covers the search radius. Cells don't overlap, and decoding needs no neighbors.

hld-video-uber:2.prompt: Geohash uses a base-32 alphabet. Adding one more character to a geohash multiplies the number of cells covering the world by:
hld-video-uber:2.explanation: Each base-32 character encodes 5 bits, so one more character splits each cell into 2^5 = 32 sub-cells (alternating 4x8 or 8x4 arrangements). The 4 comes from quadtrees, which split each node into 4.

hld-video-uber:2.prompt: Why does a quadtree handle uneven density (dense downtown, sparse suburbs) better than a fixed grid?
options: It splits a node into four children only when it holds too many points, so dense areas get small cells and sparse areas stay coarse
It stores every point in a balanced binary tree sorted by latitude
It uses hexagonal cells, which have equal-distance neighbors
It replicates dense cells across more servers automatically
hld-video-uber:2.explanation: A point-region quadtree recursively subdivides until each leaf is under a capacity threshold, so cells adapt to density. A fixed grid either has huge downtown cells or millions of empty rural ones. Hexagons are H3, not quadtrees.

hld-video-uber:2.prompt: Why are hexagonal cells (as in H3) attractive for things like surge pricing or demand heatmaps compared with square grids?
options: Hexagons nest perfectly inside their parent cell at every resolution
Every neighbor of a hexagon shares an edge and its center is the same distance away, which makes smoothing and ring queries uniform
Hexagons can be encoded as shorter strings than squares
Square grids cannot be indexed hierarchically
hld-video-uber:2.explanation: A square has 4 edge-neighbors and 4 corner-neighbors at different distances. A hexagon's 6 neighbors are all equidistant, so k-ring aggregation and gradients behave consistently. H3 children only approximately fit their parent, and square grids can be hierarchical (quadtrees, S2).

hld-video-uber:2.prompt: A team stores drivers in PostgreSQL with a B-tree index on (lat, lng) and runs `WHERE lat BETWEEN ? AND ? AND lng BETWEEN ? AND ?`. Why is this slow at scale?
options: B-trees cannot index floating-point columns
PostgreSQL ignores composite indexes in range queries
The query needs a full table scan because BETWEEN is never indexable
The index narrows efficiently on lat only, so it scans a thin band around the whole globe and filters lng row by row
hld-video-uber:2.explanation: A composite B-tree can range-scan its leading column. The second column's range only filters within that band. Spatial indexes (geohash, GiST/R-tree via PostGIS, S2, H3) map 2-D proximity onto structures that prune in both dimensions.

hld-video-uber:2.prompt: Driver positions change every few seconds. Why do many designs prefer a fixed grid or geohash buckets over a classic quadtree for this data?
options: Quadtrees cannot answer nearest-neighbor queries
Constant moves force frequent node splits/merges and locking in a shared tree, while a grid update is just moving an ID between two buckets
Geohashes are more accurate than quadtree coordinates
Quadtrees only work for points inside a single city
hld-video-uber:2.explanation: A quadtree is great for mostly static points (restaurants), but high write churn causes restructuring and contention. With fixed cells, an update is remove-from-old-cell plus add-to-new-cell, which is cheap and easy to shard. Quadtrees do support nearest-neighbor queries.

hld-video-uber:2.prompt: In Redis 6.2+, which command returns members of a geo set within a radius or box of a point?
options: GEOSEARCH
GEOADD
GEOHASH
ZRANGEBYLEX
hld-video-uber:2.explanation: GEOSEARCH (and GEOSEARCHSTORE) replaced the now-deprecated GEORADIUS family in 6.2. GEOADD inserts points, and GEOHASH returns a point's geohash string. Under the hood a geo set is a sorted set scored by a 52-bit geohash.

hld-video-uber:2.prompt: You need drivers within 2 km of a rider using geohash buckets. Which steps belong in a correct approach? Select all that apply.
options: Pick a precision whose cell size is at least the search radius
Query the rider's cell plus its 8 neighbors
Post-filter candidates by exact distance to the rider
Treat the length of the shared prefix as the distance in meters
Query only the rider's own cell
hld-video-uber:2.explanation: Cell size bounds how many neighbors you need, the 3x3 block covers boundary cases, and exact distance filtering removes corner candidates beyond 2 km. Prefix length is only a coarse proximity hint, and querying a single cell misses nearby drivers across the border.

hld-video-uber:2.prompt: Which are genuine limitations of geohash? Select all that apply.
options: Nearby points across a cell boundary may share little or no prefix
Cell width in meters shrinks toward the poles, so cell size isn't uniform
Geohashes can't be stored in an ordinary string index
It requires a dedicated spatial database to compute
hld-video-uber:2.explanation: Boundary effects and latitude distortion are the real caveats. A geohash is just a string or integer, so it works in any B-tree, sorted set or key-value store, and it's computed with simple bit interleaving.

hld-video-uber:2.prompt: A quadtree always splits every node into four children, so all of its leaves cover equal areas.
options: True
False
hld-video-uber:2.explanation: False. An adaptive quadtree splits only nodes over capacity. Leaves in dense areas are deep and small, while leaves in sparse areas are shallow and large. That adaptivity is the main reason to use one.

hld-video-uber:2.prompt: Two points with a long common geohash prefix are guaranteed to be close, but two points only 10 m apart may share no prefix at all.
options: True
False
hld-video-uber:2.explanation: True. Sharing a prefix means both lie in the same cell, which bounds their distance. Across a major boundary (e.g. the equator or prime meridian), even very close points differ from the first character.

hld-video-uber:3.prompt: 1 million drivers are online and each sends a GPS update every 4 seconds. Roughly what write rate must the location service absorb?
options: 25,000 writes/s
250,000 writes/s
4 million writes/s
2.5 million writes/s
hld-video-uber:3.explanation: 1,000,000 / 4 s = 250,000 updates per second. This rate is why the live-location store is usually in memory (Redis or sharded in-process maps) rather than a disk-bound primary database.

hld-video-uber:3.prompt: Where should the latest position of each active driver live for matching?
options: An in-memory, geo-indexed store keyed by driver with a short TTL
The trips table in the primary relational database
Object storage, written as one JSON file per update
The CDN, so riders can fetch it directly
hld-video-uber:3.explanation: Matching needs only the latest location, read and written at very high rates. An in-memory geo index with TTL serves that. Historical pings can be streamed asynchronously to cold storage. The trips table would be crushed by 250k writes/s.

hld-video-uber:3.prompt: The nearest driver by straight-line distance is across a river with the closest bridge 5 km away. What should matching rank candidates by?
options: Haversine distance, because it is cheapest to compute
Driver rating only
Estimated time of arrival over the road network
Geohash prefix length shared with the rider
hld-video-uber:3.explanation: Geo cells give a cheap candidate set, then ranking uses road-network ETA (traffic, one-ways, bridges). Straight-line distance is just a filter. Using it for ranking produces exactly the river problem.

hld-video-uber:3.prompt: Two matcher instances pick the same idle driver for two different riders at the same moment. What prevents double-assignment?
options: Have riders refresh the app before confirming
Rely on the driver to reject the second request
Run the matchers on the same server
Atomically transition the driver from AVAILABLE to OFFERED with a conditional write (compare-and-set) and a TTL
hld-video-uber:3.explanation: A conditional update (e.g. `SET driver:42:lock rider NX EX 15` or `UPDATE ... WHERE status='AVAILABLE'`) lets exactly one matcher win. The loser moves to the next candidate. The TTL frees the driver if the offer is never answered. Running on one server doesn't remove the race.

hld-video-uber:3.prompt: The backend must instantly notify a specific driver of a new ride offer. Which transport fits?
options: A persistent connection (WebSocket/gRPC stream) or mobile push, so the server can push to the driver
The driver app polls the trips API every 60 seconds
Email notification
The driver re-sends its location and checks the response for offers
hld-video-uber:3.explanation: Offers expire in seconds, so the server needs a push channel. Long polling intervals add up to a minute of latency. Piggybacking on location pings ties offer latency to ping frequency and fails when pings pause.

hld-video-uber:3.prompt: A driver drives into a tunnel and stops sending updates. How should the system avoid matching riders to them?
options: Wait until the driver manually goes offline
Give each driver's live-location entry a TTL slightly above the ping interval so stale drivers drop out automatically
Run a nightly job that removes inactive drivers
Keep them matchable until the next trip completes
hld-video-uber:3.explanation: Expiring entries (e.g. TTL ~3x the ping interval) means silence equals unavailability, with no cleanup job. A nightly sweep or manual logout leaves ghost drivers that riders get matched to.

hld-video-uber:3.prompt: You shard the live-location store. Why shard by geography (city or cell) rather than by hash of driverId?
options: Hashing driverId would put each driver in multiple shards
Hash sharding doesn't support TTLs
Nearby-driver queries are spatial, so geo sharding keeps a query on one or few shards (with dense cities split further)
Geographic shards never become hot
hld-video-uber:3.explanation: With hash-by-driver, every 'who's near me' query fans out to all shards. Geo sharding localizes reads, but a big city can become hot, so you subdivide busy regions into finer cells. That's why geo shards are not hotspot-free.

hld-video-uber:3.prompt: Why is writing every GPS ping synchronously to the main trips database a poor design? Select all that apply.
options: It creates massive write load for data where matching only needs the latest value
Historical pings can be streamed asynchronously to cheaper storage instead
Relational databases can't store floating-point coordinates
It couples ping latency to the primary database's health
Location data must never be persisted anywhere
hld-video-uber:3.explanation: The hot path needs only the current position. History (for fare disputes, analytics, ETA models) can flow through a stream to a warehouse or time-series store. Relational DBs store floats fine, and trip routes are typically persisted for billing and safety.

hld-video-uber:3.prompt: A driver doesn't respond to a ride offer within 15 seconds. Which behaviors are reasonable? Select all that apply.
options: The offer expires and the next-best candidate is offered the ride
The driver's offer lock is released automatically by its TTL
The driver stays locked until they respond, however long it takes
The system keeps re-offering the same driver until they accept
hld-video-uber:3.explanation: Offers are time-boxed: on timeout the lock expires and matching continues with other candidates, possibly marking the driver as less likely to accept. Indefinite locks or repeated retries to one driver strand the rider.

hld-video-uber:3.prompt: Batching ride requests over a short window and solving the assignment jointly can give better overall outcomes than greedily giving each rider the nearest free driver.
options: True
False
hld-video-uber:3.explanation: True. Greedy assignment can strand a later rider whose only nearby driver was taken by someone who had other options. Solving a small bipartite matching every few seconds lowers total pickup time, at the cost of a slight delay.

hld-video-uber:3.prompt: Straight-line (haversine) distance is generally a good-enough proxy for ETA when ranking candidate drivers in a city.
options: True
False
hld-video-uber:3.explanation: False. Rivers, highways, one-way streets and traffic make road ETA diverge sharply from straight-line distance. Haversine is useful to build the candidate set cheaply, not to rank it.

hld-video-uber:4.prompt: Why model a trip as an explicit state machine (REQUESTED → ACCEPTED → ARRIVED → IN_PROGRESS → COMPLETED, plus CANCELLED)?
options: It lets the database skip indexes on the trips table
It removes the need for any concurrency control
It makes trips render faster in the mobile app
Invalid transitions (e.g. COMPLETED → ARRIVED) can be rejected centrally, keeping trip data and billing consistent
hld-video-uber:4.explanation: A transition table makes every allowed move explicit and rejects the rest, so late or duplicate events can't corrupt a trip. You still need concurrency control for simultaneous events; the state machine only defines which transitions are legal.

hld-video-uber:4.prompt: A rider taps Cancel at the same instant the driver taps Accept. How do you make exactly one of these win?
options: Process whichever HTTP request reached the load balancer first
Use conditional updates such as `UPDATE trips SET state='ACCEPTED' WHERE id=? AND state='REQUESTED'` and check the affected row count
Apply both and let the app show whichever arrives last
Lock the whole trips table during every transition
hld-video-uber:4.explanation: Optimistic concurrency on the current state turns the race into a compare-and-set: one update matches and the other affects 0 rows and is told the trip moved on. Arrival order at the load balancer isn't the commit order, and table locks kill throughput.

hld-video-uber:4.prompt: At what granularity is surge pricing typically computed?
options: Per small geographic cell over a short time window, from demand vs. available supply
Once per city per day
Per rider, from their trip history only
Globally, one multiplier for all markets
hld-video-uber:4.explanation: Imbalance is local and fast-changing: a stadium emptying affects a few cells for minutes. Cell-level (e.g. hexagon) multipliers recomputed every minute or so match that. City-wide daily pricing can't react.

hld-video-uber:4.prompt: Surge changes between the moment the rider sees a fare and taps Confirm. How do you guarantee they are charged what they saw?
options: Recompute the fare at confirm time and charge the new value
Disable surge recalculation while any rider has the app open
Issue a fare quote with an ID and expiry, and have the confirm request reference that quote ID
Store the multiplier in the client and trust what it sends back
hld-video-uber:4.explanation: The server stores the quote (price, multiplier, expiry) and binds the trip to it, so the price is locked and can't be tampered with. Trusting a client-supplied multiplier invites manipulation, and freezing surge globally is unworkable.

hld-video-uber:4.prompt: Adjacent cells show surge multipliers of 1.0x and 2.5x, and drivers cluster right on the boundary. What is a common mitigation?
options: Make cells much larger so a city is one cell
Smooth multipliers across neighboring cells (e.g. averaging over a k-ring) and limit how fast they change
Hide multipliers from drivers entirely
Recompute surge only once per hour
hld-video-uber:4.explanation: Spatial smoothing and rate limiting soften sharp edges that cause gaming and oscillation, while keeping local responsiveness. Huge cells or hourly updates throw away the locality and freshness surge needs.

hld-video-uber:4.prompt: Billing, receipts and driver payouts all react to trip state changes. How do you reliably publish those changes without dual-write bugs?
options: Write the new state to the DB, then publish to the broker in a separate call
Publish to the broker first, then update the DB when consumers acknowledge
Have each downstream service poll the trips table every second
Write the state change and an outbox event in the same DB transaction, then relay the outbox to the broker
hld-video-uber:4.explanation: The transactional outbox makes the state change and its event atomic; a relay (or CDC) publishes at-least-once and consumers dedupe by event ID. Write-then-publish loses events if the process crashes between the two steps.

hld-video-uber:4.prompt: The driver app times out and resends 'start trip' for a trip that is already IN_PROGRESS. What should the API do?
options: Return success without changing anything, treating the repeated transition as idempotent
Return a 500 error so the app knows something went wrong
Create a second trip record in IN_PROGRESS
Move the trip back to ARRIVED and start it again
hld-video-uber:4.explanation: Mobile networks retry. If the requested target state equals the current state (same trip, same driver), returning success makes retries safe. Erroring confuses the driver, and re-running the transition could reset timers or fare meters.

hld-video-uber:4.prompt: Which trip state transitions should a ride-hailing state machine allow? Select all that apply.
options: REQUESTED → ACCEPTED
ACCEPTED → CANCELLED
IN_PROGRESS → COMPLETED
COMPLETED → IN_PROGRESS
REQUESTED → COMPLETED
hld-video-uber:4.explanation: Accepting, cancelling before pickup, and finishing are the normal flow. A completed trip is terminal (corrections go through adjustments or refunds), and a trip can't complete without being accepted and started.

hld-video-uber:4.prompt: Which inputs are sensible for computing a cell's surge multiplier? Select all that apply.
options: Open ride requests in the cell over the last few minutes
Available (online, idle) drivers in or near the cell
Recent rate at which riders accept quoted fares
Total drivers registered in the city, including offline ones
hld-video-uber:4.explanation: Surge reflects live supply versus demand and how price-sensitive demand is right now. Registered-but-offline drivers aren't supply. Counting them would understate the shortage.

hld-video-uber:4.prompt: Storing the full history of trip state transitions with timestamps, not just the current state, makes fare disputes and debugging easier.
options: True
False
hld-video-uber:4.explanation: True. An append-only transition log shows who did what and when (e.g. when the driver arrived and when the trip started). That supports waiting-time fees, cancellation fees, support cases and replaying bugs.

hld-video-uber:4.prompt: Surge multipliers should be recomputed synchronously from the whole city's data on every individual ride request.
options: True
False
hld-video-uber:4.explanation: False. Surge is computed periodically (e.g. every minute per cell) by a background aggregation job and cached. Requests just read the current value. Per-request recomputation adds latency and load and makes prices jitter.
